# Algorithm classification and runtime decision review

**Scope.** Research/planning only. This classifies numeric prop updates and keyed structural updates for the retained-VDOM runtime. It does not propose that a storage choice alone demonstrates end-to-end speed. The current qualified synchronous headless comparison fails: native/React paired median geometric means are 1.0637, 1.3224, and 1.4963 at 128, 1,024, and 10,000 rows, respectively; p95 medians are 1.0223, 1.2437, and 1.0890. All 15 page pairs/7,200 frames passed correctness and timing-floor verification, but neither speed gate passed (`performance-implementation-plan.md:19-46`; raw analysis `results/current-owner-kernel-headless-v1/analysis.json`). This is one fixed all-dirty workload and one headless environment, not a general React comparison. Separate whole-page profiles include page initialization, harness/DOM inspection, layout, measured frames, and teardown, so their native prepared-row hotspot is not phase causation (`.cache/current-kernel-cpu-diagnostic-stage/README.md:30-38`; `primary-verification.json`).

The current ordinal owner kernel has a compiler-associated six-argument program consuming an existing change-record buffer and captured row inputs; it intentionally adds no second input matrix, token-index field, ordinal-copy buffer, or version registry (`performance-implementation-plan.md:84-101`). The live worktree also contains the adjacent-token cache described in the current task handoff, after the qualified kernel baseline; that adjacent cache has no timing qualification. Treat its hit rate and the cost it avoids as unknown until recorded. Current implementation facts can also be checked in `src/vdom_snapshot_runtime.ts` (prepared numeric row execution around lines 2570–2690 and 3276–3335), `src/component_state_runtime.ts` (prepared row/lane and keyed-reuse paths around lines 4900–5050 and 2770–2810), and `src/world_dirty_journal.ts:85-239` (owner/site ordered dirty membership).

## 1. Classification: this is incremental dataflow plus ordered-tree maintenance

Numeric prop updates are an instance of **incremental computation / change propagation**. A state cell or trait is a source; compiled binding metadata gives a bipartite dependency relation from source slots to projections/host props. Given changed sources `ΔS`, the runtime must find the affected projection set `A = reach(ΔS)`, compute each relevant pure projection against one coherent version, compare it with its committed output, and emit changed host writes. This separates invalidation (may need work) from value change (did work change the output) and host mutation (must a writer run). The implementation plan explicitly makes those three distinct questions and locates equality between projection and host application (`performance-implementation-plan.md:329-344`).

Keyed VDOM edits are a separate but coupled problem: maintaining an **ordered dynamic sequence** of child identities plus indexes into owner state, bindings, and host placements. Insert/remove/move can be cheap in the sequence representation yet still expensive if they force full-list enumeration, owner discovery, binding-index repair, or host placement. A correct hybrid therefore shares one identity/version/lifecycle contract and one prepare/validate/host/publish boundary; current plans explicitly flag that sparse deltas and numeric kernels do not yet compose into one path (`performance-implementation-plan.md:320-327, 452-478`).

### Symbolic end-to-end cost model

For one flush, let:

- `U` = input writes/dispatches; `S` = dirty sources; `D` = changed dependency edges; `A` = unique affected sinks; `P` = projection executions; `E` = equality checks; `W` = host writes; `V` = owners visited for validation/lifetime/identity; `I` = index entries read or rewritten; `H` = structural edits; `Q` = queued/acknowledged changes; `G` = allocated bytes/objects and resulting GC work; `Cprep` = amortized cold preparation/compilation/cache build.
- `c_x` are measured per-operation costs on the actual JS engine/runtime/host. They are symbols, not guessed constants.

A useful decomposition is:

`Tflush = Cprep/Nreuse + c_dispatch·U + c_dirty·Fdirty(S) + c_gather·Fgather(S,D,A) + c_dedup·Fdedup(A) + c_project·P + c_equal·E + c_validate·V + c_host·W + c_ack·Q + c_alloc·G + c_structure·Fstructure(H,I) + Cfixed`.

`Fdirty` includes journals/dirty-set membership and version/coalescing rules. `Fgather` includes edge walks, row/token gathers and index lookups. `Fdedup` includes duplicate sinks and repeated source notifications. `Fstructure` includes sequence edits, key/owner/binding-index maintenance and DOM insert/move/remove. `Cprep/Nreuse` amortizes compiler work, descriptor construction, token creation, bucket build, and JIT warmup over actual reuse; it must also be reported as startup/memory when reuse is not long. `G` is not safely inferred from allocation count alone because collection/GC pauses and object shape/retention matter. The model must preserve global ordering, coherent input versions, all-projections-before-host-writes, and acknowledge only after successful host commit.

Lower bounds matter: if every one of `N` rows has `k` changed props, exact output requires at least `Ω(Nk)` projection-result decisions and `Ω(W)` host writes; no sparse index, tree summary, or CSR layout makes a truly dense update sublinear in output. If only `h` keys move and each changed subtree has size `z`, the achievable structural lower bound is at least `Ω(h + changed host placements + changed index records)`; logarithmic sequence lookup does not remove the need to update affected owner/binding/DOM state.

## 2. Candidate algorithms and where they fit

| Family | Work model / strengths | Appropriate workload | Risks / evidence status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Compiled affected-edge traversal** (CSR/adjacency lists or direct emitted writers) | `O(S + D + A)` conceptually; compact integer edge arrays reduce pointer-chasing/dispatch; direct writers remove generic lookup/projector calls. | Sparse/moderate dependencies, fixed or slowly changing graph, compiler-known topology; potentially work proportional to affected sinks. | Build/index cost and dedup can dominate; many changed inputs can revisit shared sinks; JavaScript loop and typed-array overhead must be measured. Notebook Experiment Q says generated writers beat the dense plan interpreter in every run in one narrow repeated-host fixture, while explicitly not establishing whole-runtime superiority (`research.ipynb`, Experiment Q). Earlier graph/scan/bucket sweeps find topology-dependent winners, not one universal graph win (`research.ipynb`, Experiments A/A2/A3). **High confidence** that compiler knowledge is useful; **low confidence** on integrated benefit.
| **Dirty-owner/site journal or dirty buckets** | Queue exact dirty membership (`O(S)` plus membership); bucket scan cost proportional to touched bucket slots, not just changed cells. Clustered changes can turn scattered edge work into sequential scans. | Clustered dirty owners, repeated site writes that coalesce, intermediate densities; stable owner layout. | Per-entry maps/linked nodes/tokens impose pointer chasing and retention; bucket size is distribution-sensitive. Existing `world_dirty_journal.ts` makes owner-major order and reuses memberships, but does not itself show runtime speed. Experiment A3 reports different graph/bucket/full-scan winners by density and distribution; no universal threshold is justified (`research.ipynb`, Experiment A3). **Medium confidence** in the mechanism, low on chosen bucket geometry.
| **Dense row/column pass** | `O(N·k)` sequential-ish iteration; avoids sparse gathers, duplicate removal and branch-heavy membership. SoA columns can batch one scalar field and enable compact buffers. | High dirty fraction, same component/layout, homogeneous numeric state/props, especially when most outputs change. | Dense path pays for untouched rows at low density. Per-row objects/closures/properties can erase native typed-array expectations. Current all-dirty measured path remains slower than React at 1,024/10,000 despite prepared-row kernel correctness (`performance-implementation-plan.md:35-46, 91-117`): dispatch reduction alone has not crossed the whole-page cost. **High confidence** that dense is necessary as a workload family, not sufficient for advantage.
| **Sparse matrix / incidence representation (CSR, CSC, bitsets, tiles)** | CSR source→sink fanout gives contiguous edge traversal; CSC sink→source supports validation/projection grouping; bitsets make union/intersection word-parallel in native code but JS BigInt/typed-bit loops need separate measurement; blocked/tiled incidence trades index overhead for locality. | Large stable dependency graph; CSR for push propagation; CSC for pull/validation; bitsets when universe is bounded and dense enough for word operations; tiles when activity clusters by owner/component. | Maintaining both orientations duplicates state; dynamic structure triggers costly index repair. A full Boolean matrix costs `O(S·A)` space and is a dead end except tiny bounded graphs. JS has no automatic SIMD semantics guarantee from typed arrays; data size, JIT, bounds checks, element kind, and host calls determine outcomes. Prefer one canonical compiled incidence/index representation and derive only the minimal auxiliary index justified by phase counts. **Low-to-medium confidence** pending browser-engine traces.
| **Object-backed bounded buckets for ordered keys** | Hash key lookup plus local shifts bounded by bucket capacity; whole-order scan is linear over occupied slots. | Local moves/inserts/removes in long keyed lists, while retaining order and key identity. | Needs bucket splitting/rebalancing and key→slot repair; repeated slots still shift within a bucket; sparse DOM work can dominate. Project’s Experiment AT/AU supports bounded object buckets against `findIndex/splice` and indexed flat arrays on localized moves, but excludes renderer integration. `src/columnar_keyed_region.ts:1-24, 77-145` implements linked leaves, a key map, local `splice`, and iteration; the experiment found a parallel-array bucket candidate did not improve edit latency or scan speed (paper abstract and appendix §8.17; `research.ipynb`, Experiments AT/AU and columnar follow-up). **Medium confidence** as ordered-sequence primitive; not proof of mixed UI speed.
| **Flat array + key map** | Fast simple scan and low conceptual overhead; key lookup expected O(1), but ordered insertion/removal shifts suffix `O(N)` and an index map may require suffix rewrite. | Small lists, mostly append/tail changes, or when simplicity/scan dominates and measurements support it. | Head/middle edits invalidate positions. The indexed-array control in Experiment AU is the fairer competitor and makes index rewrite cost explicit. Avoid “array + map” claims that omit suffix repair.
| **B+ tree / rope / finger tree / order-statistic tree** | `O(log_B N)` path to a key/order statistic, bounded node splits/merges; summaries can aggregate subtree lengths/dirty counts. | Very large ordered regions with frequent bounded middle edits, rank/offset queries, and traces proving the current bucket implementation scans/repairs too much. | More indirection, split/merge logic, node allocation, balance metadata, and harder iteration; DOM placements and owner/index updates remain. Ropes were designed for text edits/summaries, not evidence of a UI win. Existing plan says compare first to bucketed storage and require bounded edits to show total-owner/sibling/index scans before changing tree (`performance-implementation-plan.md:522-535`). **Low confidence / defer** until structural traces identify a sequence-maintenance bottleneck.

### Sparse versus dense is an execution choice, not a storage fork

Keep compiler/dependency identity as the semantic source of truth; select a traversal over it. A preparation-time known homogeneous program can choose generated row code or dense column execution. A sparse run can walk a dirty queue / CSR adjacency. A clustered middle-density run might inspect only marked owner buckets. Runtime density selection is justified only if its cost to count/estimate, switching behavior, and worst-case tail are charged to the same flush; the existing plan prefers compiler-time choices absent evidence (`performance-implementation-plan.md:187-198, 515-520`). A practical boundary is not a hard-coded percentage: measure the crossover surfaces by `N`, `S/N`, fanout, cluster shape, row heterogeneity, and `W/N` on the actual engine, then either specialize by compile-time-known shape or add the smallest validated estimator.

## 3. AoS versus SoA in JavaScript

**AoS** (one row object containing values/props/state) naturally matches owners and heterogeneous JSX rows. It makes lifecycle, keyed lookup, and sparse per-owner changes understandable, but dense updates may touch many object headers/properties and execute polymorphic code. **SoA** (separate typed columns for value, version, flags, prop slot) permits homogeneous numeric loops and avoids allocating a wrapper per scalar. It fits compiler-proven numeric lanes and repeated row programs; the project already has typed numeric columns and stable numeric cells as candidates, but package/correctness evidence is not timing evidence (`performance-implementation-plan.md:490-513`).

Do not import cache-line claims from C++ as if they predicted V8 behavior. JS object layouts, hidden classes/dictionary transitions, pointer compression, GC tracing, JIT tiering, bounds checks, typed-array implementation, and calls into DOM/host APIs all intervene. In fact, separate project inspection found numeric cells changing to accessor/dictionary storage under activation; the shared-prototype-accessor candidate preserves fast-property shape, but has no timing verdict (`performance-implementation-plan.md:246-250`). This makes JS engine object-shape evidence more relevant than an assumed native cache-line model. Treat layout as a hypothesis tested by actual engine traces and end-to-end runtime timing.

**Recommendation:** one logical owner/site identity and one authoritative version/lifetime contract, with physical SoA columns only for compiler-certified homogeneous primitive slots; retain object-oriented owner metadata and generic fallback for heterogeneous/dynamic values. Do not duplicate a mirror state that requires extra publish/ack/version choreography. The task’s requested heuristic “SoA for numeric props + object buckets for structure” is directionally consistent with the research paper, but remains a candidate; the more recent object-bucket versus parallel-array mechanism study specifically warns that SoA does not automatically improve the ordered structure itself.

## 4. Unified representation and limited execution plans

Use one compiler/runtime plan envelope and one ownership tree/VDOM as the semantic representation: stable owner/site/key IDs; typed state/binding slots; source→sink dependency metadata; keyed-region delta capabilities; host writer descriptors; version/lifetime provenance; and debug spans kept out of hot loops. Keep committed VDOM snapshots inspectable. Runtime caches (prepared tokens, lookup maps, dirty queues, key indexes) must be derived, invalidatable, and non-authoritative. Structural edits update the same owner/binding indexes and enter the same candidate validation and publication transaction. This follows the retained-VDOM/DAG separation in `paper.md:108-128, 141-160` and the shared-state constraints in `performance-implementation-plan.md:187-200, 320-327`.

Limit to three execution plans over that representation:

1. **Compiled dense homogeneous kernel:** known layout, direct reads/writes, minimal dispatch/gather; use only when expected work is dense/homogeneous. Maintain existing validation, equality, host failure, reentry and ack semantics.
2. **Sparse affected-frontier executor:** dirty-source/owner queue plus compiled outgoing dependency records; deduplicate affected projections, project once per coherent cut, equality-filter, then batch writers. Candidate use for sparse updates. Do not add a redundant inverse index without phase evidence.
3. **Keyed structural delta executor with generic VDOM fallback:** consume proven insert/remove/move/replace deltas, maintain ordered buckets and only affected owner/binding/host mappings, then commit through the same transaction. If proof fails (filter/sort/opaque transform/unknown key), generic keyed reconciliation evaluates the region.

An adaptive “smart” executor is not a fourth representation. It is a policy among these plans only after its counters and selection cost are recorded; no separate VDOM, dirty/version universe, or acknowledgment protocol per plan. Cold setup must be costed against reuse and memory. Eliminate duplicate state only if the remaining authority clearly owns mutation, versioning, invalidation and publication.

## 5. Sequence indexes and the right role for B+ trees

A B+ tree offers bounded fanout and cache-friendly page-like nodes in systems with controlled allocation/layout, but JS arrays inside object nodes still have engine-specific layout and GC costs. A rope/finger tree additionally maintains summaries; useful summaries could be subtree size, dirty-owner count or visible priority. Those summaries can make queries/selection incremental, but every mutation must update them and every affected DOM placement still has to be committed. Current object buckets already bound local shifts; the observed parallel-array keyed candidate did not outperform them. Thus the next question is not “would a B+ tree be asymptotically better?” but “does a real delta path still spend time proportional to total siblings, and is that the critical phase?”

Use stable key→bucket/slot identity and explicit anchors for proven edits. If key position is reindexed after local shifts, count those writes. If key lookup maps to an ordered-tree leaf/slot, include map updates/splits. When a move affects only order but not owner identity/props, ideally avoid rebinding; prove whether host movement can be expressed as a bounded set of placement ops. Global sort/filter is fundamentally broader and should stay on a general path unless the collection semantics support incremental ordering.

## 6. Confidence and falsifiable assumptions

| Claim / assumption | Confidence | Falsifier or needed observation |
|---|---|---|
| Latest qualified owner kernel is slower than React in the frozen all-dirty workload at all sizes under test (ratios above 1 at all three medians). | High for this exact build/workload/environment; low external validity. | A properly matched independent registered reproduction would revise the environment-specific claim; sparse/structural workloads are not covered by this result. |
| Whole-page profiles identify the dominant hot phase. | Low; they explicitly include harness, mount/layout/teardown and have minified offsets. | Source-mapped phase-isolated CPU/allocation recordings that reconcile to uninstrumented timing, with matched per-phase counters. |
| Adjacent-token cache reduces current runtime cost. | Unknown; current live cache is adjacent to a qualified baseline but itself unmeasured. | Cache hit/miss, validation/rebuild, saved scans, allocation/retention and elapsed phase cost on cold/warm and stale-token cases. |
| Sparse exact frontier beats dense traversal below a useful crossover. | Medium as an algorithmic expectation; low on crossover location. Graph/scan/bucket notebook sweeps show size-, density-, and cluster-dependent winners. | Integrated pairwise comparisons with actual `S,D,A,P,W`, cluster shape, and maintenance cost; an online switch may lose even if one path wins when selected post hoc. |
| Columnar numeric state lowers authored JSX cost. | Low-to-medium; lane correctness and prior fixed-topology column evidence exist, but current kernel failure and unresolved author-path integration preclude a broad claim. | Same authored TSX, same host writes and semantics, phase counts, cold+steady timing, and ordinary state/setter path; compare columns against stable-cell and object row layouts. |
| Bounded buckets help local keyed edits. | Medium for collection mechanism, low for browser runtime. Mechanism studies exclude reconciliation/DOM. | Delta-driven integrated workload with owner/binding index visits and DOM move counts; compare object bucket, indexed array, and generic React path. |
| B+ tree/rope would improve keyed runtime. | Low. Current evidence has not attributed a sequence-order scan as the remaining bottleneck. | Full mixed trace shows bucket maintenance proportional to N and accounts for a material portion of elapsed time; B+ prototype must reduce the same end-to-end phase without harming scans/GC/startup. |
| JS SoA automatically inherits C++ locality benefit. | Very low; inappropriate premise. | Actual engine inspection/benchmarks may show benefit for a named compiled kernel; there is no general transfer rule. |
| Equal projections can always skip host writes. | High for immutable primitive values; low for mutable object identity unless fields are tracked. The plan preserves conservative object writes (`performance-implementation-plan.md:338-344`). | Compiler/host contract proves immutability or compares relevant fields without missing mutation. |

## 7. Exact causal recordings required before choosing implementation

For each workload arm, make an uninstrumented latency run and a separate instrumented diagnostic on the identical locked production source/build. Keep browser timing records free of tracing overhead. Record cold preparation/mount separately from warm steady-state, and memory/allocation separately from latency. Preserve failures and timer-floor outcomes.

Per flush, collect aggregate distributions (counts and sampled timings, not per-operation logging) for:

- Input writes, public dispatches, source IDs, repeated writes coalesced, dirty owner/site count, dirty bucket count, queue/index lookup operations.
- Dependency edges read, candidate sinks gathered, duplicate sink encounters, dedup operations, unrelated owner/index visits, row/token lookups/hits/misses/stale validations/rebuilds; for the adjacent-token cache, count hit/miss/rebuild and scans avoided.
- Projection executions by type, projections with unchanged results, equality policy/cost, changed values, host-write enqueue count, actual host calls by prop/writer, bytes/values gathered/copied, host failure/reentry/retry outcomes.
- Validation checks, versions read/written, stale cuts declined, all-projection barrier and publication/ack work; exact acknowledgement batch sizes and failures.
- Structural operations by insert/remove/move/replace, keys and anchors, owner/subtree creates/disposals, bucket slots shifted/splits/merges, map/index entries written, list enumeration length, binding attach/detach, host placements, DOM operations.
- Allocations by class or sampled allocation bytes (queues, tuples, closures, maps, token records, projections, DOM staging); retained heap before/after and GC events/pauses. Avoid using sampled CPU profiles to claim wall-time attribution.
- Phase elapsed times from input to dispatch, dirty discovery, gather/dedup, project/equality, validation, host writes, acknowledgement/publication, and separate mount/layout/paint only if the claim concerns visible frames. Verify that phase sums explain total within instrumentation error and compare against uninstrumented totals.

Workload descriptors must include `N`, source/sink fanout distribution, changed fraction, random versus contiguous/clustered IDs, number of distinct sinks, outputs actually changed, keyed edit count/type/location, changed-subtree size, structural versus prop mix, homogeneous/heterogeneous rows, host capability, and reuse duration. This makes the costs explanatory instead of merely correlating elapsed time with “sparse” or “dense.”

## 8. Finite experiment decision tree (no new arbitrary thresholds)

1. **Reconfirm baseline only if the source/build differs from the frozen qualification.** Lock current exact artifact and compare matched all-dirty 128/1,024/10,000 workload; otherwise cite existing fail and proceed. Do not re-label prior results.
2. **Attribute the current path.** Capture the causal counters and phase ledger above for: dense all-dirty homogeneous numeric props; sparse numeric source updates with low/moderate/high fanout; clustered versus spread dirty owners; keyed single local move, head/middle/tail insert/remove, and mixed structural+per-frame props. Include cold prepare and steady reuse. If phase costs do not reconcile, fix measurement before representation changes.
3. **Numeric execution fork.** If elapsed work is dominated by source/edge discovery, compare sparse frontier and dense/dirty-bucket traversal over the same canonical dependencies. If dominated by row/token gather or dedup, test one cheaper compiler index or remove the specific copy/lookup only when correctness preflight remains intact. If dominated by projection dispatch, compare generated kernel/direct writers with interpreter using identical inputs/outputs. If equality dominates, verify how often it can eliminate writes. If host/style writes dominate and nearly all outputs change, stop optimizing propagation: compare host update strategy or accept the output lower bound. If allocation/GC dominates, compare reusable scratch and existing layout before adding a new queue/index.
4. **Keyed-structure fork.** If a single proven delta still visits/reindexes O(N) siblings/owners, first integrate the existing bounded bucket candidate with compiler-emitted deltas and count all writer/host index maintenance. Compare against indexed flat array and generic reconciliation on the same structure sequence. Only if sequence maintenance remains a material O(N) phase after bucket integration, prototype B+ tree/rope summaries against those same buckets. If host placements/changed subtree dominate, a new sequence index is the wrong optimization.
5. **Composition fork.** Combine winning numeric and keyed plans through one candidate transaction on mixed frames; instrument reentry, stale input, thrown host write, removal, and lifecycle semantics. If the plans require parallel version/ack state or two commits, reject the integration architecture and simplify the shared state boundary first.
6. **Decision.** Retain the simplest plan that wins on the identified workload including cold preparation, allocation/GC, semantic validation, and tail behavior. If none improves total cost, preserve generic path and stop the redesign. Any future product claim uses the already-defined matched integrated gate and the required independent-device replication; these notes create no new thresholds or preregistration.

## 9. Ranked redesigns and dead ends

**Highest expected value, pending attribution:** (1) phase/counter instrumentation and exact operation ledger, because the latest verified end-to-end path fails and profiles do not isolate cause; (2) consume compiler-proven collection deltas inside the existing owner/VDOM transaction to eliminate full-list rediscovery in mixed updates; (3) use compile-time-selected sparse versus dense execution over one canonical dependency/identity model; (4) use compiler-certified SoA only for homogeneous numeric lanes if the authored setter path and host stage benefit after full cost accounting. The implementation plan itself prioritizes reviewing the whole-cut kernel, then removing full-list/owner rediscovery while retaining one state layout (`performance-implementation-plan.md:187-198`).

**Local tweaks to withhold until attributed:** removing repeated lease checks (safety regression documented at `performance-implementation-plan.md:48-57`); more prepared tokens/maps/caches without hit/miss and retention evidence; new direct-writer mode before compiled-source binding/index work is counted; larger cache/bucket capacity tuning from microbench alone; kernel fusion claimed from op-count reduction; and parallel-array/SoA keyed buckets despite the experiment not improving edit/scan latency.

**Dead ends / bad premises:** “a DAG is faster than scanning”; “sparse means few dirty sources even when each has huge fanout”; “typed arrays imply SIMD/cache wins”; “a map makes ordered-array edits O(1)”; “a B+ tree makes a full output change sublinear”; “the key diff is the whole cost of structural UI”; “columnar and bucketed independently winning microbenchmarks compose automatically”; “fewer source lines/tests imply less maintenance”; “equal object identity implies equal projected contents”; and “lower synchronous commit time means smoother/presented frames.” Existing evidence and plan explicitly constrain these claims (`paper.md:99-128, 214-220`; `performance-implementation-plan.md:329-344, 522-535`).
